blocks.prompt: The Trumpet Is Just a Long Pipe
blocks.text: A trumpet looks like one small gold horn. It is really a long pipe, bent around so it fits in your hands. If you could unbend it, the pipe would be almost five feet long. That is taller than most kids. To play it, you press your lips together and buzz them into the mouthpiece. The buzz travels through all that tubing and pours out of the wide bell. The three valves on top work like little doors. When you press one down, the air has to take a longer path, and the note gets lower. Trumpet players keep a cloth nearby, because warm breath turns into water inside the pipe.

blocks.prompt: The Buzz That Fills a Room
blocks.text: A trumpet does not make a sound on its own. You do. Press your lips together, blow, and let them flutter. That buzzing is the real sound. The trumpet's whole job is to take that small, silly buzz and turn it into something that can fill a room. Here is how it works. The buzz goes into a little cup called the mouthpiece and races down the tubing. If you straightened a trumpet out, that tubing would stretch almost five feet. At the far end the pipe flares open into the bell, which throws the sound out into the room instead of letting it rattle around inside. The three valves on top change how long the pipe is. Press one down and a hidden loop of extra tubing opens up. A longer pipe gives a lower note. A shorter pipe gives a higher note. With three valves and careful lips, a player can reach every note in a song. Trumpets are made of brass, which is copper and zinc melted together. Brass bends into curves without cracking, and it does not rust.

blocks.prompt: Three Buttons That Changed Music
blocks.text: For most of history, the trumpet was a signal, not a melody. Ancient trumpets were straight metal tubes with no buttons and no moving parts. Two of them, one silver and one bronze, were buried with the Egyptian king Tutankhamun more than three thousand years ago. Later, trumpets called armies to move, announced kings, and warned towns of danger. They were loud, and loud was the point. The problem was that a plain tube can only play a small set of notes. A player changes notes by tightening or loosening the lips, but the pipe itself will only cooperate with certain pitches. The notes that were available sat far apart at the bottom of the range and crowded closer together near the top. That meant a trumpeter who wanted to play an actual tune had to climb into the highest, most difficult notes of the instrument, where the sound is hardest to control. Around 1818, two German musicians patented a solution: valves. A valve is a button that redirects air through an extra loop of tubing hidden in the instrument. Press it, and the pipe gets longer. A longer pipe plays lower notes. Three valves, used alone or in combination, give seven different pipe lengths, and seven lengths are enough to fill in every gap. Suddenly the trumpet could play any melody, in any key, anywhere in its range. It stopped being a signal and became a voice. Everything the trumpet is famous for now, jazz solos, movie themes, marching bands, sits on top of that small mechanical idea.

notes: The standard trumpet is pitched in B flat
Its tubing is about four feet ten inches

Three valves give seven pipe lengths

blocks.prompt: Why Three Buttons Are Enough
blocks.text: Blow air across the top of a bottle and you get one note. Fill the bottle halfway and you get a different one. The pitch depends on the size of the air column inside, and a trumpet is the same idea stretched out to almost five feet and folded three times so a human can hold it. The player's buzzing lips set the air column vibrating. The column decides which vibrations it will accept. A tube of a fixed length does not accept just any pitch. It accepts a specific ladder of notes called the harmonic series, and the rungs of that ladder are unevenly spaced. Down at the bottom the notes sit far apart, with enormous gaps between them. Higher up they crowd together until they are close enough to form a scale. This is why Baroque trumpeters, playing valveless instruments in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, had to perform their melodies in the punishing top register, where the notes were finally close enough to make a tune and where a single tired lip could ruin a concert. The valve solved this by changing the length of the pipe instead of asking the player to climb higher. Each valve diverts air through its own loop of extra tubing. The first valve lowers the pitch by two half steps, the second by one, the third by three. Used alone and in combination, the three valves produce seven different tube lengths, and seven harmonic ladders overlapping each other cover every note in between. That is the entire trick. A trumpet is not a complicated machine. It is one pipe that can be seven pipes. Even the shape of the bell has a job. A tube with a flat open end reflects most of the sound back inside instead of releasing it. The flare lets far more of that energy escape into the room and aims it forward, which is why a trumpet pointed at you sounds so much brighter than one pointed away. There is one more variable the player cannot fully control. Metal expands slightly as it warms, and warm air moves faster than cold air, so an instrument played hard for twenty minutes drifts sharp. Players correct this with the tuning slide, pulling it out a fraction to lengthen the pipe. Every performance involves quietly adjusting the length of the instrument while it is being played.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Silver and bronze trumpets were buried with Tutankhamun
Valves patented in 1818 by Stolzel and Bluhmel
Bach wrote brutally high trumpet parts in the Baroque clarino style
In Krakow a trumpet call sounds hourly and stops mid note
Dizzy Gillespie's bell was bent upward at 45 degrees
Mutes push the tone from bright to muffled and back

blocks.prompt: The Instrument That Was Almost Nothing But a Pipe
blocks.text: Strip a trumpet of everything decorative and you are left with a tube of brass, folded to be portable, wider at one end than the other. There is no reed, no string, no keyboard, no hammer. There is not even a part that vibrates on its own. Every sound a trumpet has ever made was produced by a pair of human lips, buzzing. The instrument only amplifies and shapes what the body already did. That is worth sitting with, because it explains both why the trumpet is so old and why it took so long to become useful for music. Old is an understatement. Two trumpets, one silver and one bronze, were sealed into Tutankhamun's tomb over three thousand years ago, and both were still playable when they were unearthed in the 1920s. For most of the millennia in between, the trumpet's role was announcement rather than art. It signaled the start of battles, the arrival of rulers, the hours of the day. In Krakow, a trumpet call still sounds from a church tower every hour and stops abruptly in the middle of a note, a tradition said to commemorate a trumpeter who was struck down mid warning. The instrument's job was to be heard across a valley, not to move an audience through a melody. There was a physical reason for that limitation. A tube of fixed length will not vibrate at just any frequency. It vibrates at a specific set of frequencies determined by its length, called the harmonic series. The spacing between those available notes is wide at the bottom of the range and progressively narrower toward the top. A player on a valveless trumpet therefore had two options: stay low and play only a handful of widely separated notes, or climb into the extreme upper register where the harmonics finally sit close enough together to form something resembling a scale. Baroque composers, Bach among them, wrote for specialists who lived in that punishing high range, a style called clarino playing. The skill was so demanding that when the tradition lapsed, the parts became nearly unplayable for a century. The fix arrived around 1818, when two German musicians patented the valve. The idea is almost embarrassingly simple. A valve is a piston that, when depressed, routes the air stream through an additional loop of tubing built into the instrument. Longer tube, lower harmonic series. The first valve lowers the pitch by two half steps, the second by one, the third by three, and because they can be pressed in combination they produce seven distinct tube lengths. Seven overlapping harmonic series fill every gap. A single pipe becomes, functionally, seven pipes, and the trumpet gains access to every note in western music without the player ever leaving a comfortable range. The consequence was not merely technical. An instrument that can only announce will be given announcements to play. An instrument that can play anything gets handed the melody, and then the solo, and eventually the entire emotional weight of a piece. Within a century of the valve, the trumpet had become the lead voice of jazz, an idiom built on individual expression, where Louis Armstrong turned a signaling horn into a personal voice recognizable in three notes. Players kept modifying it. They stuffed mutes into the bell to strangle the tone into a whisper or a snarl. Dizzy Gillespie spent decades playing a horn whose bell tilted upward at forty five degrees, an accident he decided he preferred because he could hear himself better. All of it, the whole history, sits on one unglamorous fact: the length of a pipe determines what it can say.
